name: Ledger Anomaly Detection
title: Ledger Anomaly Detection
answer: Ledger anomaly detection is the practice of finding entries, patterns or relationships in accounting data that do not fit what the surrounding records would lead you to expect. It sits inside continuous audit and assurance, where the point is to catch problems while the period is still open rather than months later at year end. The anomalies themselves are varied: duplicate payments, split invoices that sit just under an approval threshold, round-number postings, unusual posting times, vendor and employee details that overlap, and journal entries made outside the normal close cycle. The work is not only about fraud, since error, misposting and process breakdown produce the same kinds of outliers.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Ledger anomaly detection is the practice of finding entries, patterns or relationships in accounting data that do not fit what the surrounding records would lead you to expect. It sits inside continuous audit and assurance, where the point is to catch problems while the period is still open rather than months later at year end. The work is not only about fraud, since error, misposting and process breakdown produce the same kinds of outliers.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is the general ledger and the subledgers around it, plus the supporting tables that give an entry its context: vendor master, customer master, employee records, approval hierarchies, bank details and user access logs. These arrive as extracts from an ERP or accounting system, often as flat files or a database pull, and are refreshed on a schedule that matches how often the audit team wants to look. Because the same vendor or employee can appear under slightly different spellings or identifiers, a good deal of the setup work goes into cleaning and matching records before any detection runs. The output side is usually a dashboard or a case queue where an auditor can review flagged items, and that queue has to be small enough to be worked.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Most programmes combine several approaches rather than relying on one. Rules and thresholds catch the obvious cases, such as payments just below an approval limit or entries posted on a weekend. Statistical and machine learning models then look at the shape of the data, either by learning what normal looks like for a given account or process and scoring departures from it, or by learning from past confirmed cases where those exist. Network and relationship analysis adds a further layer by looking at links between vendors, employees, addresses and bank accounts, which is where collusion and shell company patterns tend to show up. The flagged items are then triaged by a person, because a model can rank suspicion but cannot establish what actually happened.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Anomaly detection produces leads, not conclusions, and the distance between the two is where most of the risk sits. A flag is not evidence of wrongdoing, and treating it as such can damage a supplier relationship or an employee's position before anyone has checked the facts. The data feeding the models is often personal and sometimes sensitive, so access, retention and the lawful basis for processing it all need to be settled before the work starts, and the audit trail of what was run, on which data and when, matters if findings are later challenged. Provenance cuts both ways: the auditor needs to be able to explain how a model reached a score, and the underlying ledger extract needs to be traceable back to the system it came from. Where a model was trained on historical cases, any bias in those cases carries into what gets flagged.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward detection that runs continuously rather than in periodic sweeps, with flags raised close to the moment a transaction is posted. That shifts the auditor's role further toward triage, investigation and judgement, and away from running the checks by hand. Explainability and documentation are likely to matter more, not less, as findings move from an internal note into a working paper or a conversation with management or a regulator. The harder problems are less about model choice and more about data quality, entity matching across systems, and keeping false positives low enough that the queue stays credible. As detection becomes routine, the interesting question becomes what an audit team does with a signal it cannot yet explain.
